title: Nylon vs Glass Arrays and the 400-per-cm² Patent Line
summary: See why plain nylon membrane arrays suit radioactive labels but not two-colour fluorescent ratio assays, how dense Affymetrix GeneChips are, and what the Affymetrix patent on arrays above 400 oligonucleotides per square centimetre claimed — and why, under United States law, it has expired.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 70 Hits 5 (Affymetrix density; in-house arrays above 400 features/cm² and Affymetrix patents) and 9 (nylon macroarray drawbacks) and Traps 1 (nylon and two-colour assays) and 3 (in-house arrays and patents). Checked against Cooper 2001 and Földes-Papp 2009 (Europe PMC full text), the Lipshutz 1999 abstract, US patents 5,744,305, 5,445,934 and 6,734,012 (USPTO scanned PDFs, read as page images) and 35 U.S.C. 154 with its editorial notes (Cornell LII). Sources read give GeneChips as “hundreds of thousands” or “at least 300,000” oligonucleotides in 1.28 × 1.28 cm; the reviewer’s exact “400,000 in 1.6 cm²” was not found (lesson flag). The patent claim exists, but its US term ended no later than 2012, so Trap 3’s warning is outdated (register flag proposed); Philippine patent law is not covered. “Precludes” two-colour work on nylon is qualified: a 2004 patent describes low-fluorescence nylon bonded to glass (register flag proposed). Not taught: the 3-month-to-1-year licence wait and the other Number Vault rows (table not taught in full); the Tofano 2006 Southern patent case study could not be read (PDF behind a captcha).

objectives: Explain why plain nylon membranes suit radioactive labels but not two-colour fluorescent ratio assays, and why glass does.
State the approximate oligonucleotide density of Affymetrix GeneChips and what Affymetrix patent 5,744,305 claimed.
Explain why building an array in-house is not a patent loophole and why the 400-per-cm² patent line is now outdated in the United States.

scenes.title: Two plans for a cheap array
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a research laboratory wants to save money. Plan 1: run a two-colour (Cy3/Cy5) tumour-versus-normal comparison on spare nylon membrane macroarrays. Plan 2: build its own light-directed oligonucleotide chip at well over 400 features per cm², but someone warns that “Affymetrix owns that density”. Question token: “Will the nylon work, and is the patent still a barrier?”

cues.text: Invented scenario. A lab wants a cheap array experiment. Plan one: compare tumour and normal RNA with two fluorescent dyes on spare nylon membrane arrays.
Plan two: build its own high-density oligonucleotide chip, with well over four hundred features per square centimetre.
Someone warns that Affymetrix owns that density. Will the nylon work, and is the patent still a barrier?

props.label: Nylon OK? Patent still a barrier?

scenes.title: Two surfaces: nylon and glass
scenes.altText: Schematic: two array supports side by side. Nylon membrane (porous; high DNA-binding capacity; filter arrays read with ³²P/³³P labels on a phosphorimager; two samples compared only with duplicate filters or by stripping and rehybridising). Glass slide (non-porous; rapid, reproducible target access and washing; low fluorescence background; fluorescent labels allow several targets to be hybridised to one array at the same time).

cues.text: Two classic array surfaces. Nylon membranes are porous and bind a lot of DNA, and nylon filter arrays were usually read with radioactive phosphorus labels.
With a single radioactive label, two samples can only be compared on duplicate filters, or by stripping and rehybridising the same filter.
Glass is non-porous, so targets reach the probes and wash off quickly and reproducibly, and glass has a low fluorescence background.
Because glass arrays use fluorescent dyes, two differently labelled samples can be hybridised to the same array at once and compared directly.

scenes.title: Why fluorescence fails on nylon
scenes.altText: Schematic: a scanner beam hits a nylon spot. Card 1: nylon (a polyamide) emits its own light-stimulated fluorescence and scatters light. Card 2: if that background falls in the dye’s emission band, it interferes with detection and lowers sensitivity, so nylon found wide use in isotopic, not fluorescent, assays. Card 3: isotopic labelling cannot multiplex; reading two samples at once on one array needs distinct fluorescent dyes, so two-colour ratio work is a glass method. Token: a 2004 patent describes low-fluorescence nylon bonded to glass slides — the problem is plain nylon membrane.

cues.text: Why not simply use fluorescent dyes on nylon? Nylon itself gives off fluorescence when the scanner light hits it, and it scatters light.
When that background glow falls in the same wavelength band as the dye, it interferes with detection and lowers sensitivity. So nylon found wide use with radioactive labels, not fluorescent ones.
A radioactive label cannot read two samples at once on one array; only distinct fluorescent dyes allow that. So two-colour ratio experiments are a glass-array method.
One nuance: a 2004 patent describes low-fluorescence nylon layers bonded to glass slides. The problem is plain nylon membrane, not every possible nylon product.

scenes.title: Density and the 400/cm² patent line
scenes.altText: Card: Affymetrix GeneChip — light-directed synthesis on glass; up to hundreds of thousands of different oligonucleotides; one 2001 review: at least 300,000 in a 1.28 × 1.28 cm area (about 1.6 cm²). Card: US patent 5,744,305 (Affymetrix, granted 1998), claim 1 — planar, non-porous support; >400 different oligonucleotides/cm²; each in a predefined region; ≥4 nucleotides. Card: a US patent gives the right to exclude others from MAKING, using or selling the invention — building in-house is not a loophole. Card: term limited to that of patent 5,445,934 (filed 1992, granted 29 Aug 1995); for applications filed before 8 Jun 1995 the term is the greater of 17 years from grant or 20 years from the earliest filing → ended no later than 2012. Hook answers.

cues.text: Affymetrix GeneChips are built by light-directed synthesis on glass and hold hundreds of thousands of different oligonucleotides. A 2001 review gives at least three hundred thousand in a square 1.28 centimetres a side, about 1.6 square centimetres.
Now the patent. Affymetrix patent 5,744,305, granted in 1998, claims an array of different oligonucleotides on a flat, non-porous support at a density above four hundred per square centimetre.
A patent is the right to stop others making or using the invention, so building the chip yourself was no loophole. But patents expire: this one could not outlast an earlier patent granted in 1995.

Under the United States rule for applications filed before mid-1995, that term ended no later than 2012. So in the hook, the nylon plan fails, and the patent warning is out of date, under United States law.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Nylon macroarrays work fine for two-colour ratio assays” (✓ plain nylon fluoresces and scatters light; two-colour work is done on low-background glass); “Building a high-density array in-house avoids patents” (✓ a patent covers making and using, not only buying); “The >400 features/cm² line still applies today” (✓ that 1990s US patent term ended by 2012; check current patents and local law).

cues.text: Trap one: nylon macroarrays work fine for two-colour ratio assays. No: plain nylon fluoresces and scatters light. Two-colour work belongs on low-background glass.
Trap two: building a high-density array in-house avoids patents. No: a patent lets its owner stop others making or using the invention, not just selling it.
Trap three: the four-hundred-per-square-centimetre line still applies today. No: that United States patent term ended by 2012. Check current patents and local law.

scenes.title: Noisy room, quiet room, rented fence
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Nylon is a NOISY room: it hums with its own glow, so you cannot hear two whispered colours. Glass is the QUIET room where two dyes can be compared. The 400-per-cm² line was a RENTED fence: the lease (patent term) has run out.” Tokens: noisy = nylon · quiet = glass · rented fence = expired patent. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: nylon is a noisy room. It hums with its own glow, so you cannot hear two whispered colours. Glass is the quiet room. And the four-hundred line was a rented fence whose lease has run out.

Where it breaks: nylon still works well with radioactive labels, and low-fluorescence nylon-on-glass slides were developed; and the expiry is United States law for one patent family, so newer patents and other countries, including the Philippines, need their own check.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Plain nylon glows and scatters → two-colour ratio work on low-background glass”, “Affymetrix US patent: > 400 different oligos/cm² · making counts · term over by 2012”.

cues.text: Plain nylon membranes glow and scatter light, so two-colour fluorescent ratio work belongs on low-background glass, and the Affymetrix patent claiming more than 400 different oligonucleotides per square centimetre covered in-house arrays too until its United States term ran out by 2012.

props.label: > 400 oligos/cm² patent · making counts · over by 2012

explanation.what: Plain language: early arrays were dots of DNA on nylon sheets read with radioactivity. Nylon glows faintly under a scanner’s light, which drowns out fluorescent dyes, so experiments that compare two samples with two coloured dyes moved to glass, which is smooth, non-porous and dark. Affymetrix then built chips with hundreds of thousands of short DNA probes, and patented arrays denser than 400 different probes per square centimetre; that patent has since run out in the United States. Scientific terms: nylon (polyamide) membrane, filter/macroarray, ³²P/³³P labelling, phosphorimager, autofluorescence, light scattering, two-colour (Cy3/Cy5) ratiometric hybridisation, non-porous support, light-directed (photolithographic) synthesis, feature density, patent claim, right to exclude, patent term (35 U.S.C. 154), terminal disclaimer.
explanation.why: Background fluorescence in the dye’s emission band interferes with detection and lowers sensitivity; isotopic labels cannot be multiplexed, so comparing two samples on one nylon filter means duplicate filters or stripping and rehybridising. A patent grants the right to exclude others from making, using or selling the claimed invention, so making an array in-house is covered; the term is limited by statute and by any terminal disclaimer.
explanation.measure: GeneChip: hundreds of thousands of different oligonucleotides; at least 300,000 in 1.28 × 1.28 cm (about 1.6 cm²) in a 2001 review. US 5,744,305 claim 1: planar non-porous support, more than 400 different oligonucleotides/cm², each in a predefined region, at least 4 nucleotides long. Term: limited to that of US 5,445,934 (filed 30 Sep 1992, granted 29 Aug 1995); for applications filed before 8 Jun 1995 the term is the greater of 17 years from grant or 20 years from the earliest US filing, so it ended no later than 2012.
explanation.differs: Nylon filter array (porous, high binding capacity, radioactive, one sample per filter) vs glass microarray (non-porous, low fluorescence background, two dyes on one slide); plain nylon membrane vs engineered low-fluorescence nylon/glass composite; a patent claim vs who makes the array; a patent in force vs an expired one.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick the substrate for a two-colour ratio experiment (glass), give the reason nylon is unsuitable (autofluorescence and porosity), or recognise the 400 features/cm² Affymetrix patent line. Know that the reviewer frames it as a current risk; the source text shows that US term has ended.

takeaway: Plain nylon membranes glow and scatter light, so two-colour fluorescent ratio work belongs on low-background glass, and the Affymetrix patent claiming more than 400 different oligonucleotides per square centimetre covered in-house arrays too until its United States term ran out by 2012.

questions.stem: A laboratory wants to compare tumour and normal RNA labelled with two different fluorescent dyes on the same array. Which support is most appropriate?

options.rationale: Correct. Glass is non-porous with a low fluorescence background, so two differently labelled samples can be hybridised together and compared directly.
Incorrect. Nylon gives off its own fluorescence and scatters light, which interferes with dye detection; nylon filter arrays are typically read with radioactive labels.

options.text: A nylon membrane read with ³²P and a phosphorimager
options.rationale: Incorrect. A single radioactive label cannot read two samples at once; comparison needs duplicate filters or stripping and rehybridising.
Incorrect. It is also a porous membrane support, not the low-background glass used for two-colour work; nitrocellulose also binds nucleic acids non-covalently and becomes brittle.

questions.stem: Why are plain nylon membranes poorly suited to fluorescent array assays?

options.text: Nylon gives off light-stimulated background fluorescence and scatters light, interfering with dye detection
options.rationale: Correct. Background emission overlapping the dye’s band lowers sensitivity, which is why nylon found wide use in isotopic rather than fluorescent assays.

options.text: Nylon binds too little DNA to give a signal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Nylon has a high DNA-binding capacity; its problem is background, not capacity.

options.text: Nylon cannot be used for hybridisation at all
options.rationale: Incorrect. Nylon membranes are widely used for hybridisation, for example with radioactive probes.

options.text: Nylon is non-porous, so targets cannot reach the probes
options.rationale: Incorrect. Nylon membranes are porous; glass is the non-porous support.

questions.stem: Affymetrix US patent 5,744,305 (granted 1998) claims oligonucleotide arrays on a non-porous support at more than 400 different oligonucleotides per cm². Which statement is accurate?

options.text: While in force, it could cover an array a laboratory made itself, but its US term ended no later than 2012
options.rationale: Correct. A US patent gives the right to exclude others from making and using the invention, and this patent’s term was tied to an earlier patent granted in 1995, which under the pre-1995 rule ran at most 17 years from grant.

options.text: Making the array in-house was always outside the patent
options.rationale: Incorrect. The right to exclude covers making and using, not only buying or selling.

options.text: It still restricts in-house arrays today
options.rationale: Incorrect. Under United States law its term has ended; newer patents would need a separate check.

options.text: It applied to porous nylon membrane arrays
options.rationale: Incorrect. Claim 1 requires a planar, non-porous solid support, such as glass.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 70 Hit 5 and Trap 3 say in-house arrays above 400 features/cm² “may infringe” Affymetrix patents and advise budgeting for a licence. The claim exists (US 5,744,305 claim 1, > 400 different oligonucleotides/cm² on a non-porous support), but its term was tied to US 5,445,934 (granted 29 Aug 1995) and under 35 U.S.C. 154(c)(1) ended no later than 2012. The warning is outdated for that patent family (register flag rv-affymetrix-density-patent-expired).
The patent content in Hit 5 and Trap 3 is United States law; Philippine patent rules are not covered.

Ch. 70 Hit 9 and Trap 1 say nylon autofluorescence “precludes” two-colour ratiometric assays. Sources read support that plain nylon’s background fluorescence and light scattering interfere with fluorescent detection and that two-colour work is a glass method, but a 2004 patent (US 6,734,012) describes low-fluorescence nylon bonded to glass slides intended for multiplex fluorescent use; the absolute wording applies to plain nylon membranes (register flag rv-nylon-two-colour-qualified).

Ch. 70 Hit 5 gives “up to 400,000 different oligonucleotides in 1.6 cm²”. Sources read give “up to hundreds of thousands” (Lipshutz 1999 abstract) and “at least 300,000 in 1.28 × 1.28 cm” (Cooper 2001); the exact figure was not found and density varies by chip generation.
